name: @org/source
// typecheck: The root project has TypeScript files of its own — `vitest.config.ts` and `vitest.workspace.ts` — and until 2026-08-05 no compiler saw them, because they belong to neither a library nor an application. Same defect as `lesson-42`, one floor up: there a project went untypechecked, here the gap BETWEEN projects did. The configuration lives in `tsconfig.root.json`, not `tsconfig.json`: a file under the latter name at the root takes over the whole repository in the editor and in every tool that searches up the tree.
// check-typecheck: The typecheck gate walks the whole graph, so like `check-docs` it lives in the root project. `inputs` name EVERYTHING it reads: TypeScript files (the denominator), tsconfigs (the compiler programs) and `project.json`, `package.json`, `nx.json` (the graph, including targets inferred by plugins). The patterns are global because a new project has to be covered from its first commit — a hard-coded list would drift at the first new library, and the gate would be the one to stop seeing, not CI to fire.
// check-tokens: The token gate (names, tiers, pairs) lives in the root project rather than in `tokens`, and not for convenience: it reads package ENTRYPOINTS (`libs/components/*/ng-package.json`) and the library STYLESHEETS, while `tokens` is a dependency of `components` and not the other way round — so a change in the library does not make the tokens project affected. A removed entrypoint with `component.<name>.json` left behind would slip past the gate built partly for that. The root project is affected by every change (measured in `lesson-47`), so this gate always runs. `dependsOn` on the tokens build is hard: the gate compares ARTIFACTS in `dist` against the DTCG sources and without them has nothing to compare. Stylesheets are in `inputs` for point 7: it asks what the library REALLY paints, so a new `background:` declaration has to invalidate this cache — otherwise the first unmeasured color would ride through on a cache hit.
// check-parts: The parts inventory gate lives in the root project for two reasons at once. First it reads `docs/components/*.md` — the **Parts** tables are the only surface where a consumer ever sees that inventory — and `docs/` belongs to no library, so a target in `components` would not move when only a card changes. Second, the root project is affected by EVERY change (measured in `lesson-47`), and this gate guards the public styling API: the day it does not run is the day a part disappears without a trace. `dependsOn` on the library build is hard — the second reading of the inventory takes `ɵcmp` from the built package, not from sources, and without it has nothing to compare.
// check-browsers: The browser matrix gate lives in the root project although it is about `sandbox-e2e`, and not for convenience: it reads `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (point 5 — which engines the workflow installs and whether `e2e` is on the list at all), and a workflow belongs to no application. A target in `sandbox-e2e` would not move when only CI changes, leaving it blind to exactly the way of shrinking the matrix that leaves no trace in the Playwright configuration. The root project is affected by EVERY change (measured in `lesson-47`), so the gate always runs. `inputs` name everything it reads: the e2e configuration and policy, the spec files (the denominator of point 3), the workflow and `project.json` (the `e2e` target is INFERRED by `@nx/playwright/plugin`, so its command comes from the graph, not from a file). No `dependsOn`: the measurement goes through `playwright test --list`, which starts neither a server nor a browser — and the probe in point 6 asks about engine behaviour, not about this library.
// check-language: The language gate lives in the root project because its denominator is the WHOLE git index — no library owns that, and a target inside one would be blind to every file outside it. Hence `inputs` of `{workspaceRoot}/**/*`: any file at all can carry a second language, so any change has to invalidate this cache. `dependsOn` on the library build is hard — the public-surface limb reads `dist/libs/components`, and a translated source with a stale artifact is exactly the state it exists to catch. One thing it CANNOT hash: `/usr/share/dict/polish` and `/usr/share/dict/american-english` live outside the workspace, so a changed dictionary does not invalidate a cached run. The canaries of point 1 answer for that on every real run — but a cache hit executes nothing, so the honest statement is that the dictionaries are trusted between runs and measured on each one.
// check-reach: The reach gate walks the WHOLE git index from a list of roots, so it lives in the root project for the same reason `check-language` does: no library owns that denominator, and a target inside one would be blind to every file outside it. Hence `inputs` of `{workspaceRoot}/**/*` — a file added anywhere is a file to reach, and a line deleted anywhere can be the last thing that pointed at one, so any change has to invalidate this cache. No `dependsOn`: the measurement is over the repository, not over anything built from it — the walk reads sources, configuration and documentation, and `dist` is not tracked.
// check-support: The support policy gate lives in the root project because it reads `docs/support.md` — a document belonging to no library, so a target inside `components` would not move when only the policy changes, which is exactly the drift point 2 exists to catch. It is the one gate here with `cache: false`, and for a reason no `inputs` list can fix: point 4 reads GIT — the release tags and the commit subjects since the newest one — and git history is not a file pattern. Amending a message to add the `!` of a breaking change touches no file at all, so a cached run would answer from a measurement taken before the breaking change existed. The run is a handful of file reads and two `git` calls, so the price of always running it is smaller than the price of listing what it reads and being wrong.
// check-docs: The documentation gate: every promise in docs/ names a gate and its reference control, and the named paths exist and run in CI. It lives in the root project because `docs/` belongs to no library — which is what makes a documentation change mark this project affected. The comment sits HERE rather than in `targets`: there a value must be a target object, and a string blows up the Nx graph (`lesson-43`).
